candidates.title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
candidates.introExcerpt: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

candidates.title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
candidates.introExcerpt: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.

candidates.title: Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space
candidates.introExcerpt: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation -- doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within sim 1.3M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at 2times higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/

candidates.title: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes
candidates.introExcerpt: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.

candidates.title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates
candidates.introExcerpt: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.

candidates.title: Trends and Determinants of Sustainability Sukuk Issuance: Evidence from Global Markets
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: Despite the growing prominence of sustainability sukuk in the global realm of sustainable finance, little is known about the dynamics of their issuance. This study is the first to document the evolution of sustainability sukuk issuance and explore the determinants of its size. Using a cross-country sukuk dataset comprising 11,944 issuances between 2012 (i.e., the year when the first sustainability sukuk was issued) to 2022, it highlights that sustainability sukuk remains a minuscule fraction of overall sukuk markets, and its rapid growth during the last recent years is mostly concentrated in Islamic finance-oriented countries like Indonesia, Malaysia, and Saudi Arabia, while other developing Muslim-majority nations show limited participation. Examining determinants, we find that a higher security quality, a more extended debt structure, and major international currency denominations (e.g., USD and Euro) positively influence the size of the sustainability sukuk issue. Additionally, we uncover two unique drivers of sustainability sukuk issuance. The first is second party opinion, where its increased costs reduce issue size. The second is the underlying equity-based Islamic contracts, which encourage larger issuances compared to sale-based contracts. Our results also indicate that issuances by government entities and financial institutions, and those raised for social purposes rather than green projects, tend to be larger. Lastly, we find that a higher level of economic development and greater reliance on international trade in the issuing country may lead to a larger issue size. This paper concludes by calling for policies and incentives to encourage future sustainability sukuk issuance.

candidates.title: Islamic Social Financial Instruments and Sustainable Community Development: Evidence Synthesis on Community Resilience
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: This study investigates how Islamic Social Finance (ISF)—through zakat, waqf, and sadaqah—supports sustainable community development by strengthening economic, social, institutional, psychological, and environmental resilience. Using a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis of 93 studies published between 2010 and 2025, the paper synthesizes fragmented scholarship to identify the mechanisms through which ISF enhances resilience. Findings show that zakat provides short-term stabilization and crisis relief, waqf enables long-term asset creation and public-goods provision, and sadaqah delivers flexible emergency support. Integrated ZISWAF models, particularly those inspired by Ascarya, emerge as the most effective structure for maximizing development outcomes when supported by strong governance, institutional coordination, and digital innovation. The study contributes (i) a consolidated evidence highlighting thematic fragmentation in ISF research; (ii) an integrated conceptual map linking ISF to resilience theory and the SDGs; and (iii) a multidimensional framework explaining how ISF instruments jointly foster community resilience. Policy recommendations include strengthening governance and regulatory coherence, accelerating digital transformation, adopting integrated ZISWAF delivery models, and expanding ISF applications in environmental sustainability and climate resilience.

candidates.title: Sustainability Committees and Environmental Initiatives: Insights from Dual Banking Systems in Emerging Markets
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: Recently, companies have become more concerned with environmental sustainability, and many of them have established sustainability committees (SCs) to entrench sustainability in their strategic planning and corporate culture. Drawing upon insights from stakeholder and legitimacy theories, this study investigates the nexus between SCs and environmental initiatives (EI) in emerging markets having both conventional and Islamic banks. Applying panel regressions, we find evidence indicates that the presence of an SC is positively associated with overall environmental scores, environmental products, environmental innovations, and resource reduction. Subsample analyses reveal that, for IBs, establishing SCs significantly affects overall environmental and resource reduction scores, suggesting that SCs in IBs may primarily drive symbolic (e.g., overall environmental and resource reduction scores) rather than substantive environmental efforts (e.g., environmentally-friendly products and innovations). In contrast, SC establishment shows a significant effect across all four dimensions of EI for conventional banks (CBs), underscoring its more comprehensive role in shaping environmental outcomes within CBs. These findings have important theoretical, practical, and policy implications for bank managers, regulators, and other key stakeholders.

candidates.title: Artificial Intelligence and Big Data Strategies to Enhance Islamic Banks’ Competitiveness and Sustainable Development
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: This study investigates the impact of artificial intelligence and big data strategies on Islamic banks' competitiveness and sustainable development in Jordan, employing an integrated theoretical framework combining the Resource-Based View (RBV) and Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT). The research targets 487 managers and department heads from 15 Islamic banks, with a sample size of 214 participants selected through stratified random sampling. It employs a quantitative cross-sectional design, using PLS-SEM for data analysis. The findings reveal that AI implementation, big data analytics capabilities, and data management practices are significantly and positively associated with both bank competitiveness and sustainable development performance. Employee digital competency significantly affects competitiveness but shows no significant impact on sustainable development performance. The results provide valuable implications for banking executives, policymakers, and practitioners in implementing digital transformation strategies. The study contributes to the existing literature by integrating technological capabilities with Islamic banking principles, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding digital transformation in religious-based financial institutions. The originality of this research lay in its examination of the combined effects of AI and big data strategies in Islamic banking, particularly in the Middle Eastern context, while considering both competitive and sustainable development outcomes.

candidates.title: ICT, High-Tech Exports, and Institutions as Drivers of Bank Expansion Growth in a Dual Banking System
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: This study examines how information and communication technology (ICT) adoption, high-tech exports (HTE), and institutional quality (IQ) influence bank-level expansion growth (BEG) in 218 Islamic and conventional banks operating in 12 countries from 2010 to 2023. Using bank-level panel data analysis, the results reveal that ICT adoption is the most powerful driver of bank expansion growth, reinforcing digital transformation as a universal catalyst for efficiency, competitiveness, and outreach. While HTE alone has a limited and statistically insignificant effect, its interaction with ICT generates a significant synergistic impact, indicating that national innovation capacity amplifies the growth benefits of digitalization. Institutional quality exhibits a positive but indirect role, functioning primarily as an enabling condition that supports bank expansion—particularly for Islamic banks—through stronger governance and regulatory credibility. Comparative findings show that Islamic banks rely more on institutional integrity and technological complementarity, whereas conventional banks depend more on operational efficiency and digital maturity. Robustness checks using dynamic panel estimators confirm the consistency of these relationships. Policy implications highlight the importance of strengthening digital infrastructure, promoting high-tech innovation, and improving institutional governance to foster sustainable and inclusive bank expansion within a dual banking framework.

candidates.title: Global prevalence of impostor phenomenon in medical students: A systematic review and meta-analysis
candidates.institution: National University Toribio Rodríguez de Mendoza
candidates.introExcerpt: Impostor phenomenon (IP) is a psychological phenomenon in which successful individuals fail to internalize their achievements and fear being exposed as “incompetent.” Medical students may be particularly vulnerable to IP because medical training combines repeated high-stakes assessment, competitive peer comparison, hierarchical clinical supervision, and rapid professional identity transition, potentially affecting psychological well-being and academic performance.
candidates.conclusionExcerpt: IP was frequent among pre-licensure medical students, although pooled estimates should be interpreted cautiously because heterogeneity was substantial and prevalence varied by sampling method and geographic context. These findings support the need for standardized measurement, probabilistic sampling when feasible, longitudinal research, and rigorously evaluated interventions addressing both individual coping and institutional educational practices. Citation: Vera-Ponce VJ, Huaman-Vega CH, Zuzunaga-Montoya FE, Guerrero Uceda CI, León-Figueroa DA, Rivera-Lozada O, et al. candidates.title: “The significance of context”: Fit, friction, and function in the work lives of early career academics with ADHD
candidates.introExcerpt: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with various traits that influence individuals' experiences at work. While some may be experienced as challenging (e.g., when differences in executive function impact time management), others can be more positive (e.g., when curiosity motivates exploration and discovery). Plausibly, academia is a work environment where these positive aspects should be valued. However, ADHD is still often viewed from a medicalised perspective in workplace settings, despite the neurodiversity paradigm offering an alternative, non-pathologising way to frame these individual differences. Research has begun to explore employment experiences and outcomes for adults with ADHD; however, there is currently little data relevant to academic workplaces specifically. This qualitative study offers a critical realist analysis of interviews with early-career academics, seeking to understand first-person ADHD perspectives on establishing an academic career. Consistent with the neurodiversity paradigm, the analysis foregrounds (mis-)matches between individual 'neurotypes' and workplace environments. It also highlights an ecological view by exploring how ADHD matters both for individual careers and for collective knowledge production. Findings suggest that academia can, in principle, be a rewarding environment for ADHDers, though social and institutional pressures often inhibit this potential. Furthermore, having an 'ADHD neurotype' influences both individual career trajectories and wellbeing at work; at the same time, knowledge production at the collective level may benefit from the inclusion of ADHD academics. The findings are discussed in reference to ecological models of neurodiversity and their implications for universities aiming to facilitate neurodivergent contributions and inclusion at work.

candidates.title: Stakeholder perspectives on adolescent sexual and reproductive health service utilization in Uganda’s Busoga region: A qualitative study
candidates.introExcerpt: Adolescence is a critical developmental stage marked by rapid physical, psychological, and social transitions that have lasting implications for sexual and reproductive health (SRH) outcomes [ 1 , 2 ]. Globally, adolescents account for a disproportionate burden of unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), particularly in low- and middle-income countries [ 2 ]. In sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), recent evidence continues to highlight persistent structural, sociocultural, and health system barriers that drive low utilization of SRH services and sustain high rates of teenage pregnancy and HIV [ 3 , 4 ]. Kenyan and Ethiopian studies, for example, identify transport costs, judgmental provider attitudes, restrictive cultural and gender norms, fear of stigma, and lack of privacy as recurring obstacles [ 5 , 6 ]. In Uganda, adolescent SRH indicators remain concerning. Early sexual debut, low contraceptive uptake, and high rates of adolescent pregnancy persist [ 7 – 9 ]. Uganda’s adolescent pregnancy rate (teenage childbearing) is approximately 24% among girls aged 15–19 years, HIV prevalence among 15–19-year-olds is 2.1%, and only 15% [ 10 ]. The Busoga Region is particularly affected because of poverty, early marriage norms, and limited services [ 11 ]. Recent studies in the region confirm high non-utilization of modern contraceptives and SRH services, influenced by lack of confidence in discussing contraception, perceived inaccessibility of services, and limited interaction with community health workers [ 12 ]. Despite national adolescent health guidelines [ 13 ], utilization remains low due to stigma, lack of privacy, and misinformation [ 8 , 9 ]. Yet, little is known about how multiple stakeholders, including adolescents themselves, community and religious leaders, and healthcare providers, perceive these barriers and potential solutions within the same sociocultural context. Most existing research has focused on adolescents alone or examined isolated health system factors [ 4 , 14 ]. This study addresses that gap by qualitatively triangulating perspectives from adolescents, community and religious leaders, and health providers in the Busoga Region. This multi-stakeholder approach provides an integrated understanding of how community norms, service delivery practices, and adolescent preferences interact to shape SRH service utilization, thereby offering more nuanced insights for designing locally responsive, adolescent-friendly interventions. This integrated lens complements single-perspective studies and responds to calls for multi-level approaches to adolescent SRH in SSA [ 4 , 15 ]. To address this gap, the present study explored adolescents’ attitudes, perceptions, and preferences regarding SRH services in the Busoga Region of eastern Uganda, alongside the perspectives of community leaders and health providers. By examining convergences and divergences across stakeholder groups, the study sought to identify multilevel barriers and facilitators that can inform the design of contextually appropriate, adolescent-friendly SRH interventions. The study was guided by the Health Belief Model [ 16 ] and Andersen’s Behavioral Model [ 17 ] to understand how individual perceptions, enabling factors, and sociocultural contexts shape SRH service utilization.
candidates.conclusionExcerpt: Adolescents in Busoga are motivated to use SRH services, but intersecting sociostructural and system barriers limit utilization. Strengthening adolescent-friendly services, improving provider responsiveness, addressing misinformation, and expanding community-based delivery are essential to enhance equitable access. candidates.title: Procrastination among US college students: Prevalence and impact relative to common health and life issues
candidates.introExcerpt: Procrastination is unnecessary delay that can cause various problems. There are uncertainties around how common exactly it is among students, how much it affects them, and how its prevalence and impact compare to those of other issues that students regularly face. Accordingly, this study examines data from 65,950 students (in all degree types and stages), who were surveyed across 97 US institutions of higher education as part of the American College Health Association-National College Health Assessment (ACHA-NCHA). Students were asked about 36 life and health issues, like procrastination, career, finances, appearance, family, bullying, anxiety, depression, ADHD, sleep difficulties, allergies, and influenza. Procrastination was found to be the most common issue that students reported (functionally tied with stress), affecting 72.3% of them. Procrastination was also the issue that most often harmed students' academic performance, affecting 45.4% of them (62.7% of those who experienced it), which was several times as often as issues like finances (2.8x) and ADHD (3.5x). And, procrastination was the most common cause of significant distress compared to the other life issues, affecting 45.7% of students (63.2% of those who experienced it). These rates were higher among undergraduate students, although procrastination was a leading issue among graduate and professional students too. This sheds light on the scale of student procrastination-both in absolute terms and relative to other issues they face-and highlights the need to address it using relevant interventions.

candidates.title: Online labor trafficking and machine learning: A scoping review and research agenda
candidates.introExcerpt: Labor trafficking increasingly intersects with online environments, yet there are limited computational detection approaches. To examine existing methods and their potential applications, this article reviews literature that applies or advocates analytics and machine learning (ML) for detecting labor trafficking (LT). It synthesizes methodologies across two contexts: (a) internet-facilitated LT (IF-LT), where digital platforms enable recruitment and coordination of trafficking, and (b) online-accessible LT (OA-LT), where offline signals of trafficking can be retrieved from online sources. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, six bibliographic databases were searched between January 2002 and September 2025 and complemented with additional journals, backward and snowball searches, and expert recommendations. Of 2,151 records, we assessed 51 articles for full-text and 21 were mapped and qualitatively synthesized (14 LT-focused and 7 methodologically transferable). IF-LT research clusters around online recruitment, recruitment fraud, illicit massage businesses (IMBs), while OA-LT examines supply chains, child labor, violence indicators on social media, modern slavery disclosures and high-risk sectors such as the fishing industry. Common approaches include case studies with explainable analytics, interpretable classifiers, topic modeling and advanced natural language processing (NLP) methods like sentiment analysis, transformers and large language models; positive-unlabeled learning, probabilistic modeling, and spatial analysis. Despite attention to online LT, the review reveals a gap in quantitative applications of state-of-the-art ML to online content for LT detection. Interdisciplinary and transferable techniques developed for detecting online sex trafficking (ST) offer an adaptable pathway towards automation and law enforcement applications. Beyond methodological gaps, the review emphasizes responsible and context-aware AI, including weighted indicator modeling, remedies for class imbalance, multimodal data integration, label-efficient learning with expert annotations, and clear diagnostic reporting to support accountable deployment.
